cognate: *peḱu- 'livestock' (Lat. pecua, Ved. paśu-, Av. pasu-, Umbr. pequo) paired with *wiHro- 'man' (Ved. vīra-, Av. vīra-, Umbr. ueiro)
drift_or_renewal: Latin renews *wiHro- with pastores (Umbrian ueiro keeps it); in the slab's Vedic lines the pair is spread over livestock lists (go, aśva, aja, avi) + vīra/puruṣa, and AVŚ 11.2.18 counts puruṣa among the five paśavaḥ
shared_syntax: coordinated merism 'men (and) cattle' as object of a prayer for protection / non-harm (Lat. salua seruassis, Umbr. salua seritu, Av. ϑrāϑrāi, Ved. mā ... rīriṣaḥ / 'whoever [harms] us among horses, men, cows')
context: Cato's lustration prayer to Mars (Agr. 141) asks that 'shepherds and flocks' be kept safe: note that pastores pecuaque salua seruassis is in the context-before line (CatAgr 141.3 w1/2) of the Latin anchor, whose passage line has only 'Mars pater'. The Umbrian Iguvine prayer asks the same of 'men and cattle' with the same verb and adjective (salua seritu ~ salua seruassis); AV spells ward off harm from 'our horses, men, cows, goats, sheep' (AVŚ 12.2.29) and ask Rudra-Bhava not to covet 'our cows, our men' (11.2.45); 11.2.18 counts men among the five paśavaḥ; Avestan asks 'for protection of cattle and men'. Same ritual speech act, same two-member object. The exact pair paśu + vīra is not in a slab anchor (12.2.29 has vīra + go/avi, 11.2.18 paśu + puruṣa); it is in support (AVP 19.56 paśubhiś ca vīraiḥ, AVŚ 11.1, Avestan pasu vīra). The 'high' rating rests on that support (the Umbrian veiro pequo ... salua seritu beside Latin pecua salua seruassis, and Avestan pasu vīra) and on the recalled literature (Watkins), more than on the slab anchors alone.
phrase: *wiHrōs peḱu ... (salwom) servā- : 'keep men and cattle safe'

support.locus: Il. 1.503, 12.164, 13.631 (41 lines with Ζεῦ πάτερ in Homer)

cognate: *dyew- 'Sky (god)' + *ph₂tér 'father': Ved. dyaúṣ pitā́ (voc. dyaùṣ pítar), Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ, Lat. Iū-piter
drift_or_renewal: Latin univerbates the vocative phrase into the name Iuppiter; Greek keeps it as a two-word invocation; Vedic keeps it as a two-word epithet, mostly paired with pṛthivī mātā
shared_syntax: divine name + 'father' in apposition, typically vocative in prayer
context: Il. 15.372 (context line of both Homeric anchors) is Nestor's prayer opening Ζεῦ πάτερ; AVŚ 9.10.23 / 6.120.3 address Sky as 'our father' (dyaur naḥ pitā) in cosmological and funerary prayers; Catullus and Cato invoke Iupiter. The Homeric Ζεῦ πάτερ is formulaic (41 lines), Vedic has the exact vocative dyaùṣ pítar (RV 6.51.5). The Homeric Ζεῦ πάτερ sits in the context line (Il. 15.372) of both Homeric anchors; Catul 66.29 is cited only for 'Iupiter' in its context line (Catul 66.30), which the slab does not tokenize, so no slab lemma/etymon is given for it; Cato 132/134 in support is the firmer Latin evidence.

support.locus: Aeschylus Eum. 166; Pindar P. 8.59, 11.10; Soph. OT 897

cognate: *h₃nobʰ- 'navel' (Ved. nā́bhi-, Gk ὀμφαλός) in the phrase 'navel of the earth'
drift_or_renewal: 'earth' renewed: Ved. pṛthivī́- vs Gk γῆ/γαῖα; 'navel' cognate in root but with different suffixes (-i- vs -l-)
shared_syntax: navel-noun + genitive 'of the earth' (Ved. nā́bhā pr̥thivyā́ḥ, AV loc. pṛthivyām; Gk γᾶς ὀμφαλός, ὀμφαλὸς γῆς)
context: Both name the sacred centre where the god is installed and from which he speaks: Agni 'placed at the navel of the earth' (AVŚ 7.62.2; RV 3.29.4 'we set you down at the navel of the earth', the altar/vedi = 'end of the earth', the sacrifice = 'navel of the world' RV 1.164.35) ~ Delphi as γῆς ὀμφαλός, Apollo 'sitting on the navel of the earth' as expounder (Plato Resp. 427c), the prophetic seat (Eur. Med. 668, Ion 5). Concrete cultic sense, not anatomy, in both. Weakened by the cross-cultural spread of navel-of-the-world imagery.
phrase: *h₃nobʰ- of the earth: the cult centre where the god sits

cognate: *pótis 'husband' as object of 'find', subject an unmarried girl
drift_or_renewal: verb renewed: Ved. vid- 'find' (*weyd-) vs Gk εὑρίσκω; the Greek cognate of vid- (εἶδον) has drifted to 'see' only
context: AVŚ 2.36 is the pativedana charm for a girl to get a husband; AVŚ 14.2.45 (wedding hymn) 'the girl who finds a husband'; Od. 6.277/282, in the Nausicaa episode, the townsfolk imagined gossiping that the marriageable girl has 'found a husband' (πόσιν εὗρεν). Same social frame (the unwed daughter), same object noun. But 'find a husband' is natural idiom and Greek has it only in this one scene, so chance is not excluded.

cognate: *n̥-dʰgʷʰi-tó- 'unfailing, imperishable' (Ved. ákṣita-, Gk ἄφθιτος) with a water noun from *wed- (Gk ὕδωρ; Ved. útsa- < *ud-so- 'spring') or Ved. ap-
drift_or_renewal: the water noun differs: Gk ὕδωρ vs Ved. útsa- (same root *wed-, different derivative) or āpaḥ (renewal)
shared_syntax: adjective *n̥dʰgʷʰitó- qualifying a water / spring noun
context: Hesiod's 'imperishable water of Styx', the primeval cosmic water the gods swear by; Vedic 'the waters run ever unfailing' (AVŚ 10.6.35, context line of the anchor), the Maruts 'milk the unfailing spring' (RV 1.64.6), 'springs ever unfailing' (AVŚ 1.15). Cosmic waters in both. It is the same adjective as in śrávas ákṣitam ~ κλέος ἄφθιτον, which supports an old 'unfailing stream' collocation. Greek has it only once, and AVŚ 7.17.3 (pivot) has the adjective with 'life', not water.

cognate: *néh₂us 'ship' with a bahuvrīhi in *h₁erh₁- 'row' (Ved. -aritra-, Gk -ορος / ἐρετμός)
drift_or_renewal: suffix differs: Ved. aritra- (*-tro-) vs Gk -ορος (o-grade *-orh₁-o-) and ἐρετμός; numerals differ (śata- 100 vs ἐείκοσι 20, πεντήκοντα 50)
shared_syntax: accusative/genitive 'ship' + numeral- (or su-, nitya-) + oar bahuvrīhi epithet
context: Ved. 'the hundred-oared ship' (RV 1.116.5, Bhujyu's sea rescue; AVŚ 17.1.116 'you have mounted the hundred-oared ship for well-being'), 'the divine well-oared ship' (AVŚ 7.6.6 = RV 10.63.10) ~ Hom. 'twenty-oared ship' (Od. 9.322), 'fifty-oared ship' (Pindar, Euripides). Same epithet type built on the cognate root for the same noun. Ship and oar go together everywhere, and the slab's Greek anchor (Hel. 1267) has only ship + oars, not the compound, so: low.

drift_or_renewal: Ved. amṛta- is the subject 'the immortals' in AVŚ 7.73.6 but the drink in RV 10.123.3; Gk ἀμβροσία is the object (the food)
shared_syntax: 'lick' + amṛta/ambrosia (RV 10.123.3: rihánti ... amŕ̥tasya, partitive genitive; Ar.: ἀμβροσίαν λείχειν)
context: RV 10.123.3 rihánti ... amŕ̥tasya (they lick the immortal drink, the 'voices of the sweet amṛta') and Ar. Pax 854 ἀμβροσίαν λείχειν (she 'used to lick ambrosia among the gods') pair a cognate verb (*leyǵʰ-) with a cognate object (*n̥-mr̥-tó-) in the same relation: lick + the food/drink of immortality, in both cases what is done in the gods' world. Licking is not the usual verb for this food (Greek gods eat or drink ambrosia; Vedic gods drink amṛta), so the rare shared choice is more than generic. The slab's Vedic anchor (AVŚ 7.73.6) is related but not identical: there the immortals (amṛtāsaḥ) are the subject licking the offering. Caveats: one instance on each side, and the Greek is comic.

note: All 150 bundles read in order. 7 claims: 2 high (men-and-cattle *wiHro-/*peḱu protection prayer, Lat./Umbr./Ved./Av.; Sky Father), 1 medium (navel of the earth as cult centre), 4 low (find a husband; unfailing water; numeral-oared ship; lick ambrosia/amṛta). Dropped as generic: wolf and sheep similes, cows and sheep lists, waking and sleeping merism, pótnih₂ + mother. Most bundles pair AV verses with Greek prose and have no shared phrasing.
